payload.text: Cosmic scale and exoplanet counts make extraterrestrial life statistically plausible.
Statistical opportunity does not overcome the absence of direct evidence for alien biospheres or intelligence.
Habitability is broader than an Earth-twin model because extremophiles expand the viable chemistry space.
Complex life may require a rare chain of stable astrophysical and geological conditions.
The Fermi Paradox describes missing detection, not proof of absence.
The Fermi Paradox remains powerful because the sky is still silent after decades of search.
Search incompleteness matters because humanity has sampled only a tiny observational window.
Extremophile survival does not prove abiogenesis or complex evolution is easy on other worlds.
Abiogenesis may be common if early Earth is representative rather than exceptional.
The Great Filter remains a serious explanation for why intelligence may be vanishingly rare.
Alternative biospheres could evolve in oceans, subsurfaces, or atmospheres unlike Earth surface ecology.
Even habitable-zone planets may fail because atmosphere, magnetism, tectonics, and timing all matter.
Rare-Earth arguments assume one narrow route to complexity despite many possible planetary pathways.
Interstellar distance and energy constraints isolate civilizations and reduce the odds of detection.
Large-number statistics matter because even rare success rates become meaningful across cosmic scales.
Earth is still the only known world with life, so caution is more scientific than optimism.
Technological civilizations may be quiet, local, or hard to detect without being nonexistent.
Speculative hidden-civilization theories explain silence less parsimoniously than rarity does.
The best current inference is not certainty, but a high probability that life emerged elsewhere.
Current evidence still supports skepticism more strongly than a conclusion that life is widespread.

justification.evidence: The pro side sustained probabilistic pressure across all rounds.
The pro side answered silence and Rare Earth objections more consistently.
